Bansir and Kobbi rest by the wall of Babylon after another long day of work.
Bansir complains that his purse is always empty, although he makes fine chariots.
Kobbi admits that his purse is empty too, although he plays at every feast.
A rich man passes and Bansir asks why gold comes easily to some men and not to others.
Kobbi remembers Arkad, the richest man in Babylon, who is said to have begun with little.
Bansir overcomes his pride and the friends agree to ask Arkad in the morning.
The friends walk through the waking city towards the quiet quarter where Arkad lives.
At Arkad's gate a servant hears their request and leads them into the garden.
Arkad listens as Bansir asks why men who work hard so often stay poor.
Arkad tells them he was once a poor scribe who copied words onto clay.
Algamish the money-lender hires young Arkad to copy a long law.
Algamish asks where the scribe's silver goes, and Arkad admits that he spends all of it.
Algamish tells Arkad to keep one part in ten of everything he earns.
Arkad doubts that he can live on nine parts but decides to try for a year.
Arkad finds that nine parts are nearly enough, and his jar grows heavy.
Arkad names the first cure for a lean purse: keep one part in ten.
The second cure is to control spending by telling needs from wants.
Kobbi admits how much he spends on small things, and Arkad suggests writing every purchase down.
Algamish tells Arkad that idle silver does no work and that it should be lent carefully.
A brickmaker repays Arkad's first loan with a fair payment on top.
The fourth cure is to guard gold against loss, which Arkad learned by losing silver on jewels.
Arkad begins asking those who understand each trade before he lends.
The fifth cure is to make a home of one's own a good investment.
The sixth cure is to plan an income for old age and for the family.
The seventh cure is to increase one's own ability to earn by learning more of one's craft.
Over a simple meal Arkad reminds them that none of the cures works in a day.
The first law of gold: it comes gladly to the one who keeps at least a tenth.
The second law: gold works hard, though slowly, for a wise owner.
The third law: gold stays with the careful owner who asks the advice of the wise.
The fourth law: gold slips away when it is put into things the owner does not understand.
The fifth law: gold flees from those who demand impossible gains or follow tricksters.
Kobbi asks about luck, and Arkad tells of Hadan the potter, who found a purse of silver.
Hadan spends the silver in one season, because luck gave him gold but no habits to keep it.
Arkad shows the friends clay tablets from Nippur, written by the former slave Dabasir.
Dabasir, newly free, finds that he owes money to many people and is tempted to hide.
Dabasir asks the money-lender Mathon for help, and Mathon tells him to write down every debt.
Mathon shows Dabasir how to share his earnings fairly among his creditors.
Mathon explains that a man should borrow only what he can repay and be careful of loans for pleasure.
Dabasir is honest with every creditor, keeps his promises and finally owes nothing.
Arkad tells how he lent to camel traders, choosing with care and never lending all to one caravan.
Arkad lends to a sheep farmer and learns that gold, like a flock, grows through patience and seasons.
A stranger promises to double Arkad's silver in a month.
The wise men warn Arkad against the offer, and he refuses it.
Arkad says that gold is a tool for a good life and that the habits must be kept for years.
The friends thank Arkad and walk home through the quiet city, thinking over what they heard.
Each friend sets aside one part in ten into a clay jar for the first time.
The first months are hard, and the friends remind each other of the jars when wants pull at them.
After a year the friends return to Arkad to ask how to lend a little wisely.
After some years their purses are fatter, and their lives are calmer.
Years later the friends tell a young stranger what they learned: a habit, begun on any ordinary day.
